item.title: Some Very Rare Cats Are Feeling the Heat in Turkey
item.description:
Outside, the sun beat down on the snow-capped mountains that ring the eastern Turkish city of Van. Inside the Van Cat Research Center on a November afternoon, the air-conditioning was on full blast — just to help a roomful of silky white felines keep their cool.

With their striking mismatched eyes of blue and amber, Turkish Van cats are the pampered royalty of the city that shares their name. They’re celebrated in local folklore, honored by a giant statue on the city’s main drag and protected by the Turkish government.

Yet, these iconic cats are feeling the heat. As climate change warms eastern Anatolia, the chief caretaker at the center said finding ways to beat the heat was now nearly a year-round concern.

“We never used to use air-conditioning here,” said Dr. Abdullah Kaya, a veterinarian and professor of biology who directs the research center, which is part of Van Yuzuncu Yil University. “But eventually, because of the rising temperatures, we had to install it,” he said.

Dr. Kaya called Van cats “cold climate animals,” and added, “In the past, the warm season was very short, but now it lasts much longer, and we’ve seen changes in both their skin and their fur.”

The center has successfully rescued the breed from the brink of extinction; fewer than 100 purebred Van cats could be identified in the 1990s. Today, more than 300 roam the facility.

Climate change is warming the eastern Anatolia region of Turkey faster than the global average, according to the United Nations climate science body. Van sits about 5,700 feet above sea level, a bit higher than Denver, and is seeing warmer winters, shrinking snowpack, irregular rainfall patterns and more frequent summer heat waves.

Lake Van, Turkey’s largest lake, also is experiencing an accelerating water crisis driven by shifting weather patterns combined with water mismanagement, said Caner Yerli, an associate professor of agricultural science at Yuzuncu Yil University. Climate modeling shows the Van basin is transitioning toward a hotter, drier Mediterranean-type climate, he noted.

The Van cats are built for harsh Anatolian winters, hence their longish, cashmere-like fur. Dr. Kaya said he has seen worrisome trends. The cats’ coats are thinning more severely in the summer. He’s also noticed significant appetite loss in the summer heat, causing the cats to lose weight.

But the Van breed has one climate adaptation option not available to other felines: their most un-catlike enthusiasm for swimming.

Over the years they have been observed paddling and even diving into Lake Van. Their fur has an unusual texture that repels moisture, like a natural parka that also helps keep them dry in damp or snowy conditions.

Now, when the weather is hot, they swim in specially designed pools at the research center.

“The pools can help reduce the effects of the heat, but of course, the real problem is that climate change is happening too quickly,” Dr. Kaya said. “We need to slow it down.”

The Van cat evolved over centuries in isolation in eastern Anatolia. They gained fame in the 1950s when two Britons writing about Turkey became enamored of them. In the late 1960s, the Van cat was officially recognized as a breed.

Around the same time, rapid urbanization in Turkey was replacing garden homes with multistory apartment buildings, eliminating much of their natural habitat. Some believed Van cats could not live in apartments and abandoned them. Purebred Van cats increasingly crossbred with domestic cats.

By 1992, a survey found only 92 pure Van cats remaining in the Lake Van region, prompting the state-backed university conservation program and government restrictions on taking them out of the country.

The push to save the Van cat is fueled by Turkey’s deep cultural affinity for felines. Here, street cats are neighborhood fixtures and treated like local V.I.P.s. They nap on shop counters, stroll through mosques, sun themselves on Byzantine walls and hop rides on ferries across the Bosporus. They’ve also made Turkey a font of viral online cat content.

There was Yesim, the tabby who became famous for waiting patiently in line at a butcher shop for his daily handout of offal, and Gli, the cross-eyed resident of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul who once charmed Barack Obama.

More recently, a stray ginger stole the show when it interrupted a performance of the “Romeo and Juliet” ballet by Prokofiev.

Yet while ordinary cats roam freely, purebred Van cats have become far too precious to leave to the elements. Today, they are rarely seen wandering the streets and instead almost all lounge indoors.

Dr. Kaya said his center has not been able to conduct a scientific study on how rising temperatures are affecting the breed, though he hopes to find a partner to pursue such research. Meanwhile, he said, the air-conditioned sanctuary offers a sobering warning for Turkey’s street cats.

“Even these cats, which live in a protected and controlled environment, are suffering from the heat,” he said, adding, “Imagine how much harder it must be for cats living outside without any protection.”

Ecehan Sirali translated interviews from the Turkish for this article.

item.title: Devilish or Delightful? Krampus Is Banned From a Christmas Parade.
item.description:
The only reason Tanya Griffin put Krampus in her town’s Christmastime parade last year was because Santa was already taken. So too was the Grinch, and Jack Skellington from “The Nightmare Before Christmas.”

Instead, Ms. Griffin, the owner of a tattoo shop in Strathroy, Ontario, made a float for the local Santa Claus parade starring a shaggy and horn-wearing Krampus, St. Nicholas’s evil accomplice in central European folklore. Ms. Griffin won second place for costumes, and this year she was striving for first.

Then she found out organizers were banning her float.

The Lions Club in Strathroy said it had banned Ms. Griffin’s display from its annual parade on Saturday because it was worried that “scary costumes, rattling chains and beating sticks” would frighten children. Ms. Griffin, 43, said the concerns were overblown — and come at the cost of inclusion in a small town.

“It’s not just the float. It’s the culture,” Ms. Griffin said, referring to people of German descent who live in the area. “It’s the dismissal of an entire group of people.”

Other recent Krampus appearances have drawn controversy. Last year, a parade float in Hawaii generated criticism, while in 2024 the Archdiocese of San Antonio condemned a Krampus parade for the figure’s “resemblance to the devil.”

Krampus, frequently depicted with a whip and wearing animal skins, traces its roots to the alpine winters of Austria, Germany and nearby countries, according to Heide Castañeda, a professor of anthropology at the University of South Florida who has studied identity and rituals for 25 years.

In folklore, the monster appears alongside St. Nicholas, punishing children who misbehave. While its horns often remind people of Satan, Ms. Castañeda said Krampus had distinct origins.

Now, the figure is having a moment. Helped by social media and pop culture exposure, including a 2015 movie, Krampus clubs have sprung up across North America, organizing events and helping preserve traditions associated with Krampus. Ms. Castañeda is set to speak at the inaugural Krampus America convention in February in Florida.

“There’s been a huge resurgence in the last 20, 25 years in these traditions,” she said.

Strathroy, roughly halfway between Detroit and Toronto, is home to about 20,000 residents. Its annual Santa Claus parade, partly funded by the town, has been running for more than six decades. Locals pack downtown streets every year, said Daniel Kiekens, a real estate agent and chairman of the Strathroy Business Improvement Area.

Ms. Griffin, who owns Coven House Tattoos and Piercings in Strathroy, learned about Krampus when she was young — her birthday falls on Krampusnacht, when, according to folklore, Krampus deals with the world’s naughty.

She decided the monster was a perfect fit for the parade last year, which she said also featured floats from Starbucks and a local Pride group. “It’s not all babies and mangers,” she added.

Ms. Griffin said she received a letter last year from the nearby Calvary Pentecostal Church after Krampus appeared in the parade wearing a Santa suit, horns and ghoulish mask.

In the letter, shared by Ms. Griffin, the congregation wrote that it was disgusted by the “inclusion of satanic influences into what should have been a Christ-centered” parade.

“The Municipality of Strathroy-Caradoc must be aware of the damage these demonic forces would have on the young children of our town,” the congregation wrote.

The church did not respond to email and phone messages.

The Strathroy Lions Club said in a statement that it had dismissed the complaints it received from “certain religious groups,” but said that it had banned her float this year because Ms. Griffin had sought to “recruit a crowd of people to march through the streets, scaring people and causing chaos.”

Ms. Griffin said she had planned to have children and parents walk alongside the Krampus float wearing cloaks and antlers. She said she had also arranged for a Norwegian caroler to sing traditional alpine songs.

The club said Ms. Griffin’s float was welcome to join the parade if it was the same as last year’s.

Instead, Ms. Griffin is planning a meet-and-greet with Krampus at her tattoo shop, which sits on the parade route. She will hand out candy, temporary tattoos and coal. She expects people to dress up as Krampus in protest of the float’s omission. She said the police have told her the environment could get tense.

Jonathan Mintz, an artist at Ms. Griffin’s shop who will play Krampus, was born in Strathroy and attended the Santa Claus parade every year growing up. This year promises to be different. “It sounds like it’s going to be crazy down here,” Mr. Mintz said.

Mr. Kiekens, chair of the Strathroy business association, said he hadn’t heard complaints from local businesses about the controversy. But it has gotten people in town talking.

“Strathroy getting on the map,” he said. “Now, I’m not sure that’s what we want to be on the map for.”

item.title: Chinese-Born Neuroscientist Is Detained by ICE While Traveling From Conference
item.description:
A Chinese-born neuroscientist conducting research at Princeton University was detained on Thursday by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Washington while traveling from an academic conference, university officials and her lawyers said.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, is a third year Ph.D. student who has resided in the United States since 2016. Her visa was expired, her lawyers said, but her pending asylum application allowed her to remain in the country legally.

Via the messaging platform Slack, she informed her colleagues at Princeton’s Brody Lab that she had been detained at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while traveling home to New Jersey. But her lab mates eventually lost direct contact with her.

As of Friday, Ms. Xie was being held at an ICE processing center in Chantilly, Va. She is the latest in a string of foreign-born scientists who have been detained amid Trump administration crackdowns on foreign scientists and on immigrants more broadly.

Those policies have had a chilling effect on American research institutions’ ability to recruit and retain the world’s top minds, creating a strain on fields already struggling to enroll young researchers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” said Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

After Ms. Xie moved to the United States with her family in 2016, she went on to graduate in 2020 from the Bronx High School of Science and in 2024 from M.I.T., where she studied computer science and mathematics. Since then, she has lived in New Jersey while conducting neuroscience research as a Ph.D. student at the Brody Lab.

Earlier this week, Ms. Xie presented some of this research — on the neurons that act as a coordinate system for the brain’s mental maps — at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting in Washington.

“Eva is a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist,” the Brody Lab said in a statement on X. “She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center. She should be home.”

According to Ms. Xie’s lawyers, because her asylum application has not yet been approved and her previous visa is expired, ICE agents were alerted when she passed through an airport security checkpoint.

“In her case, as well as a number of other cases that I personally represent, we’ve seen people being arrested at domestic airports who’ve overstayed a visa but have a pending green card or asylum application,” said Kerry Doyle, one of Ms. Xie’s attorneys.

Officials from ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the grounds for Ms. Xie’s detention or whether she had been moved from the Virginia processing facility.

On Friday morning, Ms. Xie’s lawyers entered a habeas corpus filing, which formally requests that the court review whether a person’s detention is legal.

Princeton confirmed that it had arranged for Ms. Xie to receive legal counsel and would remain in contact with her attorneys, family and colleagues as the situation developed. The Society for Neuroscience said in a statement that it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to offer support.

“Our thoughts are with Eva, her family and her colleagues,” the society said in a statement on X.

item.title: White Police Officers Are Convicted of Beating a Black Man in France
item.description:
Three white police officers were convicted by a Paris court on Friday of beating a Black man in 2020 and forging a police report that wrongly incriminated him, in a case that spurred a national outcry about police conduct.

The judges who issued the verdict cited racism as an aggravating circumstance of the assault, even though the investigative judges who conducted the pretrial investigation had decided not to make it a criminal charge.

Two were sentenced to jail and the third to house arrest, and all were banned from police work. In their trial, they had acknowledged that they had assaulted and falsely accused the man, Michel Zecler, a music producer, but denied racist intent.

Serge Money, one of Mr. Zecler’s lawyers, told journalists the verdict was “a turning point,” allowing victims of police brutality to “go forward with confidence, since they can now rely on what must be called the Zecler precedent.”

The episode occurred in November 2020 after the officers stopped Mr. Zecler, now 47, to check his identity outside his studio, in part because he had contravened pandemic restrictions by not wearing a face mask. The officers ended up beating him inside his studio for several minutes.

Mr. Zecler was held in custody for two days, accused of resisting arrest, but released without charge after security camera footage showed the officers punching, kicking and beating him with a baton, without his retaliating. The officers were identified in court as Aurélien Lapersonne, Philippe Tondeux and Pierre Plantier.

At the time, footage of the assault fueled a political crisis in France and resonated globally, months after the murder of George Floyd and worldwide Black Lives Matter protests.

When it finally began six years later, the rare trial of police officers unfolded as France’s security forces faced renewed scrutiny over more accusations of brutality in response to a youth-led protest movement that has rocked the country since September.

During the trial, Mr. Zecler expressed frustration that it had taken so long for the officers to face justice. “Even with the power of the images, it took six years and then six days of trial to get the beginning of an admission from my attackers about the system that led them to lie in order to protect themselves,” Mr. Zecler said on social media.

He was hit 31 times inside his studio, according to an overview of the case by investigative judges.

Doctors said he suffered a wound to his left arm that damaged a tendon and required surgery, as well as a head injury and wounds to his scalp and lower lip, all of which incapacitated him for at least 45 days.

Mr. Zecler said this month to the French news site Loopsider, which published footage of his assault six years ago, that it had caused him “colossal damage.”

“After the punches, there’s still a lot of anger left, I think,” he said. “Why did they do that? Why did it happen that way? In reality, that’s what I really want to know.”

Though Mr. Zecler said the officers had called him racist slurs, they denied accusations of racism, and investigative judges ruled there was not enough evidence to charge them with racist intent.

But the investigative judges noted that an examination of Mr. Lapersonne’s phone had revealed “a number of remarks and jokes in truly poor taste, reflecting a number of biases based on ethnic origin.”

In its verdict, the trial court considered racism as an aggravating factor in the crimes.

There is no official tally of episodes of police brutality against Black or Arab people in France, mainly because the country forbids collecting official data on race. But in 2017, an independent official body found that young men perceived as Black or Arab were 20 times as likely to have their identities checked.

In Mr. Zecler’s case, the court found that the officers had illegally entered his private premises, the studio, without permission. Testifying in court on Tuesday, they said the incident unfolded too fast for them to understand that.

The officers said they were overcome by fear, after then finding themselves stuck in a narrow space with Mr. Zecler. They maintained that they were unable to subdue him, and had heard more individuals moving nearby.

Mr. Tondeux described the officers’ violence as “a failure,” and Mr. Plantier apologized to Mr. Zecler.

Mr. Lapersonne, who initiated the arrest, said he could not justify the six punches that he had thrown at Mr. Zecler outside his studio, but attempted to defend punching the producer inside the studio. He said he had tried and failed to subdue Mr. Zecler in a chokehold, and felt his life and those of his two colleagues had been endangered.

He said he had filed a false report of the arrest, incorrectly stating that Mr. Zecler had hit the officers, because at the time he believed that to be true.

The other two officers said they had signed off on Mr. Lapersonne’s report without thoroughly reviewing it, and filed separate complaints against Mr. Zecler because their superior suggested they do so.

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

item.title: Stand Up Straight. Eat Pizza With a Fork. This Is Butler School.
item.description:
The students wear dark suits and white gloves. They call each other “Mr.” and “Ms.,” even outside school hours. They sleep in single beds and share bathrooms in the long hallways of a 19th-century Dutch monastery.

At mealtimes, they sit together at a long rectangular table under eight chandeliers where everything, even pizza, is eaten with a fork and knife.

This is the International Butler Academy in the Netherlands, where — in the school’s words — “dreams take flight and professionalism is cultivated.” This month, 29 students finished an intensive course to learn how to be full-fledged butlers.

The butlers-to-be, ages 21 to 65, came from all over — Bulgaria, Germany, Guadeloupe, the United States — to a 135-room estate that many of them grew convinced was haunted.

The eight-week program promises entry into a gilded world. But who still seeks out a life of service fit for a century ago?

The International Butler Academy is betting that in a world where the rich are getting richer, the demand for butlers will only increase.

“Statistically, there have never been this many people who are this rich,” said Niels Deijkers, 37, the academy’s general manager, who finished the course with high marks in 2023. Many of them, he reasoned, need people to run their households.

To get into the academy in Simpelveld, a town near the borders with Belgium and Germany, applicants have to be at least 18, have a solid grasp of English and nearly $14,000 to pay for the program. No prior butling experience is required.

Roughly 60 people graduate each year. Most are men — in line with the Jeeveses and Alfreds of popular culture — but more women are enrolling in the program, largely driven by demand from the Middle East, according to the academy, which says it now routinely hosts students from Oman.

Some are sent by their employers to hone their skills. Others found the school by searching online. Among its draws was a recent video it posted that went viral, showing a “tray defense” class where students wearing jackets and ties try not to drop platters of drinks while an instructor pelts them with an oversized tennis ball.

The students’ ambitions vary. Some who completed the course this month hoped to live with rich families. Others wanted to find work on yachts or private jets.

Salvatore Fenu, 32, a Spanish student, said he came to learn “how to be a gentleman” and to “become a better person.” Having worked as a butler in villas on the Spanish island of Ibiza, he hoped for a job with an “old-money family” with the goal of retiring at 50.

Days at the academy start early and end late. Mr. Deijkers’s comments are often harsh. Pressures mount each week as students clean, iron, arrange flowers, host dinners and measure exact distances between dinner plates, napkins and cutlery. Over the eight weeks, the students have a total of seven days off.

“I’m surprised at how strict they are,” said Eva Barnard, 22, from Indiana, during a flower arranging class. (One thing they learned: To make a bouquet look perfectly round, use an odd number of flowers.)

Impassive professionalism is a must, but Ms. Barnard said she was not always able to keep her facial expressions in check. “I have a big personality,” she said. And she was “not used to getting yelled at.”

But the program was worth it to her for the ultimate goal of working in a luxury setting.

“I want to meet new people, discover more of the world,” she said.

The school was founded by Robert Wennekes, a longtime butler, in 2000. Mr. Wennekes had started recruiting butlers for rich and sometimes royal clients and found that he had trouble finding qualified candidates.

The school, citing privacy considerations, generally does not disclose where its graduate butlers go on to work. But Mr. Deijkers said that the school receives requests from retired couples in Europe, executives who travel for business and want help with their wardrobe and packing, and “noble families.”

One person known to have sought its services was the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In February, the Dutch news media reported on emails released by the U.S. Department of Justice showing the academy organizing interviews of potential staff members for Mr. Epstein in 2013, five years after he had pleaded guilty to soliciting prostitution. Mr. Deijkers said that the episode with Mr. Epstein happened long before his time.

Mr. Wennekes sold the school in 2019 to a Chinese investment company. He continued to work there until last year, leaving Mr. Deijkers in charge.

“I was incredibly strict,” he said about his time running the International Butler Academy. “Discipline was held in high regard.”

Butlers can command high salaries (often six figures) and access to a world of luxury, but that does not diminish the workload, Mr. Wennekes added. “It isn’t a shortcut to the good life.”

By this point, you may be wondering: Can you fail butler school?

Yes, you definitely can.

Graduation from the academy is based on points. A thousand points is the maximum. Six hundred are needed for a diploma. Between 500 and 600, a student receives a certificate of attendance.

Anything lower than 500 and you’ve flunked right out of butler school.

Students start with the full 1,000 points. They lose them for transgressions and can earn them back with good work. Most of them do not know their score until graduation, when they hear their final result. On average, about 70 percent of students who do the eight-week course receive a diploma, Mr. Deijkers said.

Mr. Deijkers keeps score, scribbling his observations in a notebook over the course of the eight weeks.

“The points keep you nervous,” Ms. Barnard said.

Points can be lost for substandard appearance, misspeaking or conduct deemed not butlerlike. One night during Ms. Barnard’s course, Mr. Deijkers, wearing a three-piece suit and his hair slicked back, conducted a late-night inspection of each student’s room looking for food, alcohol or an unmade bed — all of which are prohibited.

At meals, he sat at the head of the long table, pointing out etiquette violations and calling on students to give impromptu speeches.

Handling such pressures is part of being a butler, according to the school.

“People are not here to make friends, people are here to learn how to behave,” said Arnold Ilucz, of Romania, who graduated from the academy in April and took a teaching job as the school’s executive head butler.

Being away from home and separated from his wife doesn’t faze Mr. Ilucz, 29. “I’m a product of communism,” he said. “This is not suffering.”

For some students, though, the reality of butling is tougher than it seemed.

“This is the hardest I’ve worked in my life,” said Maximilian Campos, a 21-year-old from Texas. “I had the idea of butler in my head. I didn’t know if it was real.”

item.title: Maldon Salt’s Authenticity Is Questioned, Leaving Foodies Shaken
item.description:
What makes a box of flaky, artisanal seasoning worth its salt?

Culinary connoisseurs are mulling that question as scrutiny is directed at the credentials of a cult-favorite brand of salt this week.

Maldon Sea Salt, a popular flaky variety found in pantries around the world, was at the center of the shake-up. Fans of the brand, which include Nigella Lawson and Ina Garten, have lauded its taste and pyramidal shape, finishing fancy dishes or desserts with a sprinkle. Contributing to its popularity was Maldon Salt’s story as a homegrown business, founded some 140 years ago in the English town of Maldon in the county of Essex that was once a site for an Anglo-Saxon era battle. Its salt flakes, the company said, are hand-raked from the town’s River Blackwater estuary.

An investigation on Sunday by the British newspaper The Observer has complicated that image. Maldon, according to the report, was not made only with sea salt from local seawater. Trucks with rock salt imported from mines in Germany were spotted at a production facility — a fact that Maldon had not widely publicized on its packaging or its website.

The company said in response to The Observer that the imported salt came from an ancient sea, and that its “100 percent sea salt” labeling was accurate. Food regulators, including in Britain, where there is no strict definition for artisanal sea salt, approved the product.

Still, the revelation that one of Britain’s most popular artisanal brands included imported German salt rocked aficionados of seasoning.

Some took it with a pinch of salt, adding that the raw material — the inorganic compound sodium chloride — was at least authentic. Others, including food influencers, said they felt deceived, and raised questions about whether the product lived up to its premium, artisanal branding.

Then, there were those amused or exasperated by the newly nicknamed “Saltgate,” with several outlets calling it a “posh” scandal over a brand that some perceive as a status signaler. People online joked about the “salty comments.”

Salt can come in many forms: Table salt, kosher salt, sea salt, Himalayan rock salt. While common forms are industrially produced and inexpensive to buy, manufacturers of more traditional salt brands, which rely on age-old methods, can command higher prices because of their distinct texture, taste and methods.

Maldon Salt, founded in 1882, has in recent decades built a passionate following by influencers and chefs alike who often sprinkled it as a finisher over steaks, in breads or atop chocolate chip cookies. The company made about 39 million pounds, or $51 million, in revenue in the financial year that ended March 2025. (An 8.5-ounce box of salt costs about $13 at Walmart.)

Days after the investigation published, the company said it would review packaging and be more transparent about its process.

“Our previous information focused on the finished flakes and the craft of our salt makers, without giving enough detail about how we prepare our brine,” the company said on its website, adding that it took responsibility for “not sharing that story openly on our packs and website sooner.”

By Friday, Maldon’s website had been updated to include details about its “salt-on-salt” method, which it said was behind the success of the product. Seawater from salt marshes near Maldon is filtered over pure rock salt from Germany, the company said, making a concentrated brine. The mixture is then evaporated in salt pans and harvested by hand.

A spokesman for K+S, a German miner of rock salt whose trucks were spotted at a Maldon Salt facility, declined to comment on specific deliveries. But he said the supplier used rock salt deposits derived from the Zechstein Sea, an inland body of water that evaporated 250 million years ago.

The filtering process was an “essential step” to achieve the product’s signature flake, Maldon Salt said in an emailed statement on Friday. “There is no Maldon sea salt without pure rock salt.”

In Britain and in the United States, there are no specific regulations that define “sea salt” when used on labels. Other countries, such as Canada and France, have stricter rules around such labeling.

Other artisanal salt brands, perhaps seeing a marketing opportunity, posted on social media to suggest alternatives for discerning sea salt users.

“Our sea salt is made from 100 percent Anglesey seawater,” Halen Môn, a Welsh artisanal sea salt company, posted on social media Friday. “Absolutely nothing is added.”

item.title: A Chinese Tech Hub Offers a Peek at the Electric Cars Headed for Canada
item.description:
Shenzhen, the megacity in China where Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up an eight-day tour that started last week in Dublin, promotes itself as a place to see the future.

Some of what is on view, like the obvious and constant electronic surveillance, looks dystopian. But among the many impressive things in the city of 18 million is what is missing: traffic noise and exhaust fumes.

Shenzhen is China’s tech hub, but its streets offer a preview of what Canadians can expect when Chinese electric vehicles flow into the Canadian market next year at low tariffs, under a trade deal Mr. Carney and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, reached earlier this year.

Mr. Carney’s second private meeting with Mr. Xi, in advance of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, produced no new developments on Canada’s opening to Chinese autos. Mr. Carney also met with President Trump at the summit. But he returned home with an agreement under which China will reduce some tariffs on Canadian farm and fish products in exchange for Canadian concessions on some steel and aluminum products from China. And in Manila, where Mr. Carney attended the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, Canada reached the broad outline of a free trade agreement with the Philippines.

Autos did come up in China, though. Twice during the trip, Mr. Carney — who revealed during The New York Times’s DealBook Summit this week that he is a former Tesla owner — said that Canada would turn to Chinese, Japanese and European carmakers to build factories in Canada if the Detroit-based carmakers left. The trip came as the government is trying to persuade Stellantis to reverse plans to sell its factory in Brampton, Ontario, after moving production of a Jeep model from there to Illinois.

In a background document on Mr. Carney’s visit, the government said that 16,211 electric vehicles from China had been shipped to Canada since March under the lower tariff. Their arrival settled a trade war in which China had imposed high tariffs on Canadian canola.

The government did not say which brands were involved, most of the early arrivals are believed to be Chinese-made Teslas. Elon Musk’s car company said last month that it had already used up its Canadian import quota for this year.

But the government added that Transport Canada had finished crash tests and certified the safety of vehicles from two China-based companies.

The new arrivals won’t immediately bring to Canada the eerie near-silence that E.V.s have brought to Shenzhen’s busy streets, nor will they make food the predominant smell along downtown sidewalks. Only 49,000 cars, less than 3 percent of the Canadian market, will initially be allowed in at the reduced tariffs.

Several Chinese automakers have said they plan to sell in Canada, but little is known about what they will offer. (Polestar, a luxury brand owned by Geely, has had a presence in a handful of Canadian cities since 2020.)

The government wants to encourage affordable cars and is tying expansion of the quota to lower prices. It said this week that all cars from one of the certified companies would cost less than 35,000 Canadian dollars, its definition of affordable.

On Thursday, I toured several car showrooms in shopping malls near my hotel in Shenzhen’s financial district to get a sense of what may be coming.

BYD, a local company, dominates Shenzhen’s taxis. In a corner of its cramped showroom, I found the Seagull, an S.U.V. slightly roomier than the Honda Fit hatchback once sold in Canada.

Though it was the cheapest car on display, it was no grim econobox. The interior featured a large flat-panel display and an elegant, open center console like those on many Volvos. The floor model had a battery range of 420 kilometers and a price tag of 17,700 Canadian dollars.

Some features would have to be added for Canada. The car lacks a rear window defroster, and the sales clerk was unsure if it has a heat pump to keep the battery from quickly depleting in winter. The price here will most likely be much higher.

Many of the Chinese cars I saw were innovative, though perhaps not in ways that are suited for Canada. Across from BYD was Arcfox, a brand whose cars are built by a joint venture between China’s BAIC and the Canadian auto parts maker Magna International.

Its gimmick is battery swapping. When the battery of the S3 model, which costs 20,000 Canadian dollars, nears its 500-kilometer range, the driver pulls into a special garage where a robot exchanges it for a fully charged one. No one has to get out of the car, and in videos I was shown, the process appeared to take about as long as filling a gas tank. With Canada struggling to build charger networks, bringing the idea here seems fanciful.

Styling may also be an issue. For a large S.U.V. that costs about 100,000 Canadian dollars, Voyah has opted for a massive chrome grill and similarly gigantic wheels. The result resembles a Rolls-Royce caricature.

Next door, at the showroom of Zeekr, another Geely luxury brand, I found a Chinese E.V. that may prove popular here even though it is above the government’s affordability threshold. The Zeekr 007 offers an unusually high range of 688 kilometers in its base model, which costs 44,000 Canadian dollars. Telsa’s popular Model Y, by contrast, starts at about 50,000 dollars for a version with a range of 463 kilometers.

No obvious luxury features are missing from the Zeekr. When its doors open, the seats automatically slide back to ease getting out.

Whatever cars arrive from China will come with a lot of qualifications. Some models may not handle well. Their long-term reliability is unknown, as is how they will cope with Canadian winters. And Chinese brands are unlikely to have a network of parts warehouses in Canada that established carmakers rely on to ensure timely repairs.

But the streets and the showrooms of Shenzhen suggest that, at the very least, their arrival will not go unnoticed.

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

About 75 grizzly bears roam Banff National Park’s 6,641 square kilometers, but one bear stands apart. To the park’s scientists and wardens, he is grizzly bear 122. To everyone who visits or lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, he is the Boss. Despite the Boss’s fearsome demeanor, few bear experts consider him a threat to humans. Rather, they fear his celebrity may put his life and dominance in peril. Ian Austen traveled to Banff National Park, Canmore and Dead Man’s Flats, Alberta, to report on the Boss’s legend and longevity.

Read the full article.

After an appearance last year, a float depicting Krampus, St. Nicholas’s evil accomplice, will not be allowed in the Santa Claus parade in Strathroy, Ontario, on Saturday, Mark Colley reported.

From Opinion: For a lot of Canadians, and citizens of the other democracies, even this month’s Democratic tsunami in the midterms won’t be enough to immediately change their minds about the reliability of the United States, Chrystia Freeland writes.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
item.description:
Iraqi security forces were deployed on Friday in territory long controlled by the country’s most powerful Iran-backed militia, handing Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government a symbolic victory after he had threatened to dislodge the armed group.

Military and police units entered Jarf al-Sakhar, a sprawling area southwest of Baghdad, for the first time in more than a decade, the prime minister’s office said. The militia, Kataib Hezbollah, has dominated the area for years.

But it was unclear whether the group would withdraw, a crucial factor in determining whether the government can claw back power from the dozens of militias that operate in Iraq outside of its control.

Mr. al-Zaidi took office six months ago, at a time when Iraq has come under increasing pressure from the Trump administration to disarm the Iran-backed groups. He has promised to dismantle the militias by June 30, 2027.

The prime minister is moving quickly to try to gain control of the area because of concerns that fighting between Washington and Tehran could intensify soon, according to an official briefed on the negotiations between the government and Kataib Hezbollah to avoid an armed confrontation. Mr. al-Zaidi wanted to limit the group’s ability to join any return to all-out war, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

The Iraqi government had set a deadline of Friday for Kataib Hezbollah’s forces to leave the area after a government inquiry said it had corroborated intelligence reports that the group was involved in oil smuggling and pipeline tampering in the area. Mr. al-Zaidi dismissed nine security and administrative officials and ordered the armed forces into Jarf al-Sakhar. A deal was agreed before the deadline expired.

The contours of the agreement between the government and Kataib Hezbollah were still being finalized, but the deployment did not appear to be a full takeover of the area. It was unclear whether the group would be forced out entirely and whether its activities, which analysts say include arms smuggling and weapons production, would be significantly curtailed.

A plan outlined by the prime minister’s office called for an Iraqi army brigade and a federal police brigade to be deployed alongside paramilitary groups that operate under a grouping known as the Popular Mobilization Forces. The grouping is technically under the authority of Iraq’s national security forces but some militias operate with a large degree of independence and have deep ties with Kataib Hezbollah. Those links could allow the group to retain influence over strategic areas in Jarf al-Sakhar.

Mr. al-Zaidi said in an address to the Iraqi security units that were deployed on Friday that “everyone will integrate into the armed forces under one banner and one command and one law,” adding that there would be “no weapon outside the authority of the state.”

The arrangement could still allow Kataib Hezbollah to retain influence through state-aligned factions that have longstanding ties to the group, according to Lahib Higel, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group. Even so, she said, the arrival of army and police units represented real progress.

“Zaidi will still be able to sell this as a success — which it is, considering that no other prime minister has even been able to enter this location,” Ms. Higel said.

Iraq, like Iran, has a majority Shiite Muslim population. Iran-backed Shiite militias seized control of Jarf al-Sakhar from the Islamic State in 2014, after the jihadist group had swept across Iraq and captured more than a third of it. Local authorities renamed the area Jarf al-Nasr, or Bank of Victory. The fighting displaced thousands of its mostly Sunni residents, and militia forces have prevented many of them from returning.

The area has since become a largely closed military zone dominated by Kataib Hezbollah. The U.S. military said in 2020 that the group maintained heavy-rocket storage and propellant-production facilities there.

Iraqi political and militia leaders had intervened to avoid a confrontation between the government and Kataib Hezbollah. Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s elite Quds Force — an arm of its military that arms and trains militias across the Middle East — traveled to Baghdad to help mediate the standoff, according to the official briefed on the talks and an Iraqi official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions.

Mr. Qaani’s role underscored the limits of the Iraqi prime minister’s effort to curb groups closely aligned with Tehran, analysts said.

“If Kataib Hezbollah leaves Jarf al-Sakhar voluntarily, it is a modest victory for the prime minister, but ultimately, one that was facilitated by the Iranians,” said Victoria Taylor, director of the Iraq Initiative at the Atlantic Council and a former State Department official.

item.title: U.N. Fails to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons, but Plans to Try Again
item.description:
A weeklong U.N. conference on regulating lethal autonomous weapons ended on Saturday without an agreement to ban or limit use of the technology, after major military powers like the United States and Russia expressed strong resistance to binding restrictions.

Representatives of the 128 countries attending the conference in Geneva pledged to continue discussions, however, and to develop new rules regulating the use of such weapons over the next ​two years.

That outcome fell short of what a majority of states and disarmament activists had hoped the conference would achieve. They said that the need for legally binding restrictions on lethal autonomous weapons — machines that can kill without any human intervention — has grown increasingly urgent as artificial intelligence and its military uses develop at breakneck speed.

But some of the world’s leading military powers, including the United States, Russia and Israel, balked at attempts to curb their ability to develop new weapons.

Of the major world powers in attendance at the conference, only China expressed a willingness to move toward a legally binding international protocol. Ukraine, which already deploys drones with some autonomous capabilities in its war with Russia, emphasized the need for meaningful human control over such systems.

Julien Thöni, a Swiss diplomat who presided over the conference, said the commitment from major military powers to continue discussions, even at a time of severe geopolitical tension, showed that “multilateral diplomacy can still deliver” results. But disarmament activists said it was too little too late.

“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” said Nicole van Rooijen, the executive director of Stop Killer Robots, a group that campaigns against lethal autonomous weapons.

The conference, which began on Monday, was the latest in 13 years of discussions on lethal autonomous weapons held under the U.N. Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. In that time, the idea of technology that can select and attack targets without any human control has moved from the realm of science fiction into reality, as seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East.

Alarmed by the rapid development of such weapons, 163 countries voted in October in favor of negotiations on a legally binding protocol. The agreement reached on Saturday “creates a platform for discussion that leaves room for reaching a protocol,” said Bonnie Docherty, a senior arms adviser to Human Rights Watch and a lecturer on international law at Harvard Law School. “But there’s no certainty it will be legally binding.”

“States need to deliver the majority’s call for a new treaty,” she added.

item.title: In France’s Angry Autumn, TV News Channels Are Accused of Stirring the Pot
item.description:
When France erupted in nationwide protests last month, the country’s 24-hour television news channels pulled out a well-worn playbook: dramatic footage of billowing tear gas, burning cars, shattered store windows and violent street clashes, amplified by sometimes strident on-air commentary.

Now, two of the main channels, CNews and BFM TV, are under fire themselves, accused of fueling France’s autumn of discontent.

More than a million people signed a petition demanding that the French government revoke the broadcasting license of CNews, citing what they called its right-wing propaganda and racist language, content that regulators have defined as incitement to racial hatred.

At BFM TV, 160 staff members rebelled against what they characterized as a rightward “drift of opinions” expressed on air, saying in a letter to the channel’s bosses that they were ashamed to work there.

A camera crew from BFM TV was attacked by a crowd this month while covering a protest in Lyon, weeks after another crew was accosted at a memorial service for a young Black man killed by a white gunman in a working-class suburb of Paris. The city’s mayor, Ali Rabeh, put the blame for the violence squarely on the news channels, saying that they have poisoned viewers and polarized the political debate.

“It’s what people watch all day long,” said Mr. Rabeh, a left-wing politician whose parents immigrated to France from Morocco in the 1960s and who says the attack traumatized his racially diverse town, Trappes.

Neither CNews nor BFM TV responded to multiple email requests and calls for comment, but both have previously rejected charges of fomenting racially motivated violence. CNews said in a public statement about the petition that “everyone is free to criticize CNews and to challenge its editorial choices,” but that “calling for the elimination of a channel raises a fundamental question regarding pluralism and freedom of the press.”

Speaking to the French paper Le Parisien, the director of BFM TV, Fabien Namias, said his channel offered a platform to people across the political spectrum. “Hatred, racism, exclusion and division are foreign to BFM TV,” he said.

On a recent Sunday, however, two guests on the channel erroneously asserted a direct link between immigration and delinquent behavior in the protests. Last week, a commentator on CNews described Paris as a victim of “migratory submersion,” citing a plan to convert a building into a temporary homeless shelter.

Mr. Rabeh accused the channels of normalizing anti-Muslim language by giving platforms to certain far-right politicians and commentators. He said he wanted to change French law to make it harder for billionaires to own media properties, and to bolster protections for journalists who object to the political tilt of their employers. Cable news channels in the United States, Mr. Rabeh said, offered a troubling precedent.

“There are things that have to change fundamentally,” he said, “to guarantee the freedom of our journalists, to avoid an American-style drift.”

The ratings for France’s news channels are modest relative to Fox News in the United States, to which CNews is often likened because of a similar approach to culture-war issues. While Fox sometimes beats the American broadcast networks in prime-time ratings, France’s news channels have a fraction of the ratings of the leading French commercial broadcaster, TF1.

Still, their viewership has risen over the two months of student-led protests, which they have covered wall to wall. BFM TV reached an aggregate audience of 50.9 million people in October, according to Médiamétrie, a market research company, while CNews reached 44.7 million people. France’s population is roughly 70 million.

With audiences like that, these channels are destined to play an influential — critics say, divisive — role in France’s presidential election next spring. The campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron is unfolding against a combustible backdrop of social unrest, rising populism on the right and left, and fears of additional racially motivated attacks, as officials described the one in Trappes.

“The wind has shifted,” said Samuel Bouron, an expert in media at Paris Dauphine University. “It has put CNews and BFM on the defensive, and these networks are now being called upon to explain themselves, at least regarding how they shape public debates and how they regulate hate speech.”

CNews, which embraces its identity as a French Fox News, has been sanctioned or warned 20 times by France’s broadcast regulator since 2019, six times this year alone. Among the violations: airing statements that incite racial hatred, failing to offer a diversity of views and over-promoting the far right.

Still, France’s National Assembly declined to act on the petition to revoke the channel’s license, saying it was not the job of lawmakers to force a TV channel off the air. Instead, it has scheduled a debate on free speech. CNews noted that more than million signatures is far from a majority of French people.

For some critics, the challenge posed by these channels is as much about money as politics. CNews is owned by a French billionaire and media mogul, Vincent Bolloré; BFM TV, by a French-Lebanese shipping tycoon, Rodolphe Saadé. Critics said the concentration of media properties in the hands of such wealthy owners made them less accountable and more apt to reflect the politics of their proprietors.

Neither man describes himself as politically right-wing, though the output of all of Mr. Bolloré’s media holdings has a conservative angle. In testimony before the National Assembly in March, he described himself as a “Christian democrat,” without an ideological agenda.

Mr. Saadé, who is close to Mr. Macron, a centrist, told lawmakers in 2025 that he does not interfere in the editorial decisions of his holdings. That year, he visited President Trump at the White House, pledging to invest $20 billion in American ports.

BFM TV, which was spun out of an FM radio station, offers a more straight-news diet than the openly political CNews. But in August, BFM TV poached Sonia Mabrouk, a Tunisian-born French journalist, from CNews, where she had developed a reputation for interviewing far-right political figures. Ms. Mabrouk brought that specialty to BFM TV, to the chagrin of many of her new colleagues, who believed that such figures should not get that much airtime, according to two people who work there.

She did not reply to a request for comment.

Some analysts said the rightward creep of BFM TV reflected a recognition that Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far-right party, National Rally, is riding high in the polls and has a plausible path to the presidency. (The party has never entirely disavowed its founder, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and many of its candidates in recent parliamentary elections made racist or antisemitic remarks.)

“It’s not because of ideology; it’s because of interests,” said Alexis Lévrier, a media historian at the University of Reims. “They are people who have finally come to terms with the idea of a probable victory for the National Rally and show signs of compatibility with the extreme right.”

People who work for BFM TV suggest another motive: costs. Fielding a panel of talking heads is cheaper than paying for reporting in the field. The problems begin when those panels feature far-right politicians or commentators whose statements can be both inflammatory and wrong.

Thomas Leonetti, a technician at BFM TV who signed the letter of protest to the channel’s management, said he and his colleagues recognized that they had “a societal responsibility. We work at this channel, but we are also citizens and we realize the impact that such words can have in the public debate.”

“Of course,” Mr. Leonetti added, “we feel shame and embarrassment to say that we work at BFM TV today.”

Giulia Imbert and Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: On the Trail With Spain’s Prime Minister, as He Tries to Pull Out a Win
item.description:
Pedro Sánchez knows what to do to keep his position.

“I always use elbows,” Mr. Sánchez, the prime minister of Spain, said with a laugh in the corner of a locker room as he used lessons learned from his time as a youth basketball player to describe his political game.

It was minutes before a Socialist Party rally in southeastern Spain — in a packed gym fitted with basketball hoops — and a dozen days before national elections on Nov. 29. Polls suggest Mr. Sánchez, Europe’s most prominent left-wing leader, will lose after eight years in charge.

But Mr. Sánchez, known as a political survivor, appeared to relish the idea of being written off once again by the conservatives who are favored. “That is good for me,” he said in a pre-rally interview, looking relaxed in a black mock turtleneck. “It’s a good tactic because at the end of the day, they underestimate me.”

Mr. Sánchez, 54, has beaten the odds in the past, but this time, they are stacked against him.

Outside Spain, he has become a hero to the global left by resisting President Trump, welcoming migrants and denouncing what his government called Israel’s genocide in Gaza, a term rejected by Israel. Under Mr. Sánchez’s leadership, Spain has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing economies and one of its most prolific users of renewable energy. He said that he had put Spain “more in the conversation.”

Yet within Spain, many have had it with him. He has become an increasingly polarizing figure after years of corruption scandals in his inner circle, a national electricity blackout in 2025 and a migration crisis this summer in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

He tried to capitalize on left-wing frustration over spiraling rents by calling for early elections and making the issue his own. But a horrific train crash stalled the momentum that polls showed he was building, shifted voters’ attention and raised unsettling questions about his maintenance of the country’s infrastructure.

Even the online chess matches he plays to relax between campaign events are not going his way. His score of 700 on chess.com — among “the lowest,” he conceded — means his king is often felled.

For most of his career, it has been a different story. Those spurned by Mr. Sánchez, a highly disciplined campaigner, say his chiseled features and abundant charm mask a ruthless political instinct.

He mostly shrugged off regular attacks from Mr. Trump, using them to bolster his left-wing support. He joked that despite the American president “saying all these mean things about me,” Mr. Trump talked to him only about golf when they met in private. “It was weird,” he said with a laugh. The White House declined to comment.

Even Mr. Sánchez’s enemies do not believe the polls. They are traumatized by his previous comebacks, including in 2023, when he managed to assemble a governing coalition despite his party not winning the most votes.

To hear Mr. Sánchez tell it, winning has never been more important. Polling suggests that the conservative Popular Party is likely to take office after the election, in a coalition for the first time with the far-right Vox party.

“The danger is that the last time that the far right was in office in my country was during the dictatorship,” Mr. Sánchez said, suggesting that a coalition of mainstream conservatives and far-right forces risked sending Spain back to the authoritarian rule of Francisco Franco, who died in 1975. Alluding to the Spanish Civil War that installed Franco, he added, “we had of course all these terrible situations in the past.”

For Mr. Sánchez’s enemies, this is a classic stunt by a prime minister whom they portray as the primary cause of Spanish social divisions. They see his use of civil war imagery — he recorded a political ad in front of Pablo Picasso’s “Guernica,” which depicts the horrors of the war — as inflammatory.

“Less civil war, less hatred among Spaniards, less garbage from a century ago,” Santiago Abascal, the leader of Vox, who has called Mr. Sánchez a “dictator,” “traitor” and worse, said at a rally in the Canary Islands on Tuesday.

Mr. Sánchez equates Vox — which is anti-immigrant, nationalist and has challenged Spain’s acceptance of L.G.B.T.Q. rights — with the mainstream conservative Popular Party.

“Today,” he said, “they are more or less the same.”

His intention is to use the possibility of a union between Vox and Popular Party to mobilize his left-wing base — and to attract supporters of far-left parties because they think he is their only shot of averting a right-wing government.

But Mr. Sánchez also needs to peel back Spain’s exasperated centrist voters by seeming more moderate.

“This is a real referendum in favor of good politics,” Mr. Sánchez said from the stump on Tuesday night in Albacete in southeastern Spain. “And against incivility.”

The event capped a busy couple of days during which I shadowed Mr. Sánchez on the campaign trail, including in the Palace of Moncloa, the seat of the Spanish prime minister.

I ate churros with his ministers at a weekly closed-door breakfast, and caught Mr. Sánchez joking with his aides about a right-wing media conspiracy that depicted him as possessing secret tapes to drop on the opposition before Election Day. During a visit from Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fresh off his own comeback election victory, I stood with Mr. Sánchez on Moncloa’s steps as we watched the Brazilian leader delay the departure of their motorcades so he could shoot a video under the branches of a 600-year-old olive tree.

Mr. Lula had come to energize Mr. Sánchez’s campaign. The two leaders drove into central Madrid to film a conversation that had the vibe of a mutual admiration society. The Sánchez campaign quickly chopped it up into social media clips to motivate left-wing supporters.

On the sidelines, André Janones, the architect of Mr. Lula’s come-from-behind victory, applauded as Mr. Lula signed Mr. Sánchez’s red “Power of the People” campaign T-shirts. “Now, it is Spain’s turn to keep this momentum going,” he told me. And since Europe is so barren of left-wing leaders, he said, a “much greater responsibility” fell on Mr. Sánchez.

The tougher assignment for Mr. Sánchez involves bringing moderates back into the fold.

To reach them, he has replaced his far-left deputy prime minister with a more moderate economist, and taken to waving Spanish flags, long a conservative symbol, at rallies. On Tuesday evening, he dropped by the studios of Telecinco, a popular television network seen as lukewarm to the Spanish left.

Before his interview, Mr. Sánchez oozed confidence, talking with one executive, Francisco Moreno, about how he used to play basketball in Converse sneakers.

But when the interview began, the reporter pushed hard on Mr. Sánchez’s political reversals — “Evolutions,” the prime minister called them — and asked tough questions about railway maintenance and Mr. Sánchez’s decision to take a vacation during a migration crisis. Mr. Sánchez bristled after the interviewer rushed his answers so they had more time to discuss corruption scandals involving the prime minister’s associates.

“You get to speak,” Mr. Sánchez snapped. “I have the right to speak, too.”

When Mr. Sánchez walked out, his lips tightened around a forced-seeming smile. He again shook hands with Mr. Moreno and left. “The way television interviews should be,” Mr. Moreno said as he stepped into an elevator.

The next morning in a Moncloa breakfast room adorned with abstract Spanish art, Mr. Sánchez’s ministers sipped coffee from gold-rimmed cups emblazoned with the Spanish coat of arms and said their boss acquitted himself well, considering the forum. Several picked up where Mr. Sánchez had left off.

“Europe needs a strong progressive voice that continues to believe in European values,” said José Manuel Albares, the foreign minister, between bites of a Spanish pastry. Other members of the government said that they felt a sense of momentum.

They were also trying to create it. Minutes later they joined Mr. Sánchez in a room across the hall where they increased the minimum wage and raised salaries for public servants.

Later that night in the locker room, Mr. Sánchez, again in a good mood, stuck with his basketball metaphors. He said “you have to deliver” in the short time one had the ball, something he suggested other left-wing leaders could learn.

Moments later it was time to deliver again. He entered the packed gym, as supporters waved Socialist, Spanish, European and Pride flags. They cheered his litany of accomplishments and hissed at the mention of his right-wing opponents.

“Sánchez won us all over,” Pedro Arnas, 68, said after the event. But out in the country, he said, “It’s going to be tough.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting.

item.title: Who Is the Mexican Drug Kingpin Known as El Chapo Isidro?
item.description:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the United States’ most wanted criminals, has been captured, the Mexican government said on Saturday.

Mr. Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, was among the most powerful drug traffickers in Sinaloa, a state in northwestern Mexico where cartels mass produce fentanyl and other illicit drugs that are bound for the United States and other parts of the world.

The U.S. authorities have described Mr. Meza Flores as a top drug trafficker in the region who leads the Meza-Flores organization, a heavily armed and violent group. He was first indicted in the United States over a decade ago, and he has been on the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list since last year.

Here’s what we know about the drug kingpin.

Mr. Meza Flores, 44, appears to have worked his way up through the ranks of Mexico’s drug cartels. He was a leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, which split from the Sinaloa Cartel in 2008, according to the Treasury Department.

The Sinaloa Cartel, which was founded and led by Joaquin Guzmán Loera, known as El Chapo, and Ismael Zambada Garcia, known as El Mayo, is one of the world’s largest and most feared crime syndicates. Rivalries among cartels and organizations that splintered off during internal fighting have led to devastating gang wars in Mexico.

(Mr. Meza Flores shares a similar nickname but is not related to Mr. Guzmán Loera, who was arrested in 2014.)

The Beltrán Leyva split set off a bloody regional war, according to the Treasury Department, which issued sanctions against the group. Beltrán Leyva was founded by Arturo Beltran Leyva, a weapons and drug smuggler, and his brothers, and its enforcement arm is considered “one of the most ruthless and brutal in the way they dispose of their enemies,” according to the State Department.

Mr. Meza Flores later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores criminal organization.

The Meza-Flores group has smuggled tons of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States from several places in Mexico, according to U.S. officials. The group has long operated from the northern city of Guasave in Sinaloa, U.S. officials say.

In 2013, the Treasury Department officially designated Mr. Meza Flores and his group as a drug trafficking organization and linked Mr. Meza Flores’s wife, parents, sister and uncles to the criminal enterprise.

Mr. Meza Flores waged a brutal turf war with the Sinaloa Cartel, which saw the quadrupling of drug-related killings between roughly 2008 and 2012, as well as a spike in kidnappings and arson attacks, the Treasury Department said in 2013.

But the Meza-Flores group had recently allied with a faction of the cartel that has been fighting for control, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in Sinaloa’s state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars.

The Meza-Flores group is responsible for the deaths of many Mexican police officers as well as military and law enforcement officials, according to the F.B.I.

Mr. Meza Flores was indicted in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on charges related the possession and distribution of cocaine and methamphetamine. In 2019, a federal grand jury issued a new indictment for him with additional drug trafficking charges, and firearms violations.

Last year the F.B.I. added Mr. Meza Flores to its 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List, offering a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his capture.

Federal prosecutors in Washington updated the charges against Mr. Meza Flores two months ago, suggesting that the U.S. authorities were still actively pursuing him. The latest indictment added new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Mr. Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel, and it accused him of abducting and killing a member of the Mexican National Guard in Oaxaca in 2022.

Mexico’s defense ministry said in a statement on Saturday that the operation had been carried out in coordination with U.S. agencies.

The Drug Enforcement Administration said in a statement that the capture of Mr. Meza Flores “delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization” and “underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders.”

Representatives for the State Department and the F.B.I. did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw Guasave into turmoil on Friday night. Sinaloa State’s public security agency urged residents to shelter in place and stay away from a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state to avoid attacks between gang members and federal forces.

Paulina Villegas and Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Pentagon Issued Memo Limiting ‘Social Activities’ With Canadian Military
item.description:
The Department of Defense recently circulated a memo asking staff to restrict social and informal interactions between U.S. military personnel and their Canadian counterparts, Senator Mike Rounds, who was briefed on its contents, said in an interview on Saturday.

The directive is the latest sign of deteriorating relations between the allies since President Trump returned to office.

Mr. Rounds, Republican of South Dakota, said the directive was written several months ago but was only recently signed or authorized. He described it as making no changes to formal military activities but discouraged some informal or social contact between American and Canadian officers.

David McGuinty, Canada’s defense minister, acknowledged the new U.S. directive but said that it made no material difference to the vast, longstanding military cooperation between the two nations, including the world’s only joint airspace command, NORAD.

Mr. Rounds said a congressional delegation was briefed on the memo’s contents through established channels with the Defense Department’s legislative affairs office. Mr. Rounds spoke in Halifax, Nova Scotia, where the delegation is attending the Halifax International Security Forum, an annual gathering of global defense leaders.

“I think there were some social events where our officers and some of their officers were getting together in some social events, apparently,” Mr. Rounds said. “There’s a desire, I think, to put some emphasis on maybe getting some agreements on military purchases or cooperation on those types of things before we move forward with a normalization of social activities,” he added.

Mr. McGuinty told reporters in Halifax that he had been briefed on the existence of the Pentagon document but had not read it. He insisted there were no operational changes to the collaboration between the two militaries.

“I checked with our top military folks. They see no evidence of change. We continue to cooperate, we continue to work together,” Mr. McGuinty said in Halifax.

Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia, who is also part of the delegation, echoed that message.

“It’s not about NORAD. It’s about NATO. It is not about defense exercises,” she said.

Both Mr. Rounds and Mr. Kaine spoke to The New York Times in interviews on Saturday in Halifax.

He said the information allowed senators to reassure Canadian officials they were meeting during the delegation trip to the security forum, who initially feared the directive might signal a broader retreat from bilateral military cooperation.

“Once we were able to discern the negligible impact it would have on any of our relationships, it was a lot easier to explain to our Canadian counterparts,” Mr. Rounds said.

The Department of Defense said in a statement that the new guidance does not affect intelligence sharing, NORAD, or NATO operations.

“DoW is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defense of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations,” said Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell.

The existence of the memo was first reported by The Washington Post.

The document and underlying policy are the latest in a series of episodes that have strained relations between the United States and Canada since Mr. Trump returned to office. His administration has imposed steep tariffs on Canadian goods, repeatedly antagonized the country’s leaders and called into question the longstanding partnership between the neighbors.

“The tone is bad and it is unnecessary” Mr. Kaine said during a new conference, reflecting on the memo as part of a series of actions by the Trump administration that have been viewed as disruptive to the U.S.-Canada relationship.

“This is an own goal,” said Senator Chris Coons, Democrat of Delaware, who is expected to chair the Foreign Relations Committee when the Democrats take the Senate majority next year. “I’m relieved this has no significant operational impact.”

Dustin Volz contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Catherine, Princess of Wales, Documents Life With Cancer in BBC Film
item.description:
Catherine, Princess of Wales, documented her life since being diagnosed with cancer in a new film that will air this month on the BBC, Kensington Palace announced on Saturday.

Called “Heal,” the film follows the princess as she participates in the National Three Peaks Challenge, which involves hiking up the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales. Her challenge supports the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

“Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” Catherine, 44, says in a trailer for the film, which will be released in Britain on Nov. 29 and the next day in the United States. “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The princess revealed in a video in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer and begun chemotherapy, only a month after King Charles III had disclosed his own cancer diagnosis and treatment. The back-to-back announcements were a severe blow to the royal family, which has not said which cancers the princess and the king have.

Windsor Palace has said the king is still undergoing treatment, but at a scaled back pace. Kensington Palace announced in January 2025 that the princess was in remission. The cancer was detected after she was hospitalized for abdominal surgery.

The new film shows Catherine “exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness,” palace officials said on Saturday.

“The princess reflects on her own experience alongside individuals navigating their own health journeys,” the palace said in a news release. “Together, they explore the profound impact serious illness can have on the whole person, and the people, places and experiences that can help us heal.”

Catherine withdrew from public life after her diagnosis, making her first appearance several months later. At the time, in the summer of 2024, she said that “as anyone going through chemotherapy will know, there are good days and bad days.”

Since then, however, she has slowly returned to a more normal schedule for a working royal. In early 2025, she met with other cancer patients at a hospital in London. In May, she made her first official overseas trip since the diagnosis, traveling to Reggio Emilia, Italy, where she was greeted in the town’s main square by a throng of people.

The trailer for the new film shows the princess dressed in outdoor wear and a baseball cap as she hikes up the mountains.

“It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone,” she says. “Things can renew and grow. You’re nearly there. Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

item.title: Top Drug Kingpin Is Captured by Mexican Army as Gunfire Erupts
item.description:
A Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the F.B.I.’s 10 most-wanted fugitives was captured in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican government said on Saturday, in an operation that unleashed chaos as cartel henchmen and military forces clashed.

The arrest on Friday night of the drug trafficker, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro, was a major victory in Mexico’s campaign against its largest criminal organizations. Mr. Meza Flores was among the most powerful traffickers in Sinaloa, where a war between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel has killed thousands and plunged the state into relentless violence.

Mexico’s defense ministry said in a statement on Saturday that the operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores had been carried out in coordination with U.S. intelligence agencies. Representatives for the State Department, the F.B.I. and the Drug Enforcement Administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Meza Flores was a key target for the United States. He was the “dominant crime boss” in northern Sinaloa, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in the state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars for decades. Mr. Meza Flores was the top fentanyl trafficker to the United States, drawing the attention of U.S. law enforcement agencies.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw the northern city of Guasave into turmoil on Friday night as federal forces were attacked, according to a post on X by the state’s public security agency, which urged residents to shelter in place and avoid a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state.

Trucks burned across major roads and gunfire rang out in several neighborhoods, local news outlets reported. In footage shared by Mexican TV networks, helicopters flew overhead, one appearing to fire toward the ground.

A professional baseball game was suspended as gunfire rang out. Videos posted by spectators showed fans streaming into the stadium’s corridors for shelter and players suddenly running off the field. In another recording shared by a Mexican TV network, a reporter covering the clashes ducked between two cars as shooting broke out.

Mr. Meza Flores was the leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, originally part of the Sinaloa Cartel, before starting his own group, which is known as the Meza-Flores criminal organization, in Sinaloa.

The U.S. authorities describe the group as a heavily armed and violent organization that controls drug production and distribution in parts of Mexico. They accuse it of trafficking large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States.

Mr. Meza Flores was first indicted in U.S. federal court in Washington, D.C., in 2012, and a superseding indictment and arrest warrant were issued in 2019. The State Department had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.

Mr. Meza Flores’s group, previously a bitter rival of the Sinaloa Cartel, recently allied with a faction of the cartel called Los Mayos, according to Mr. López. Los Mayos has been fighting another faction called Los Chapitos for control of the cartel since 2024, after one of its founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was taken into U.S. custody.

Earlier on Friday, President Trump said he had told President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico at a summit this week in China that cartels were running her country.

“I told her that,” Mr. Trump said at a news conference. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbor.”

Ms. Sheinbaum has publicly rejected that characterization and repeatedly ruled out U.S. military intervention on Mexican soil, even as her government has deepened security cooperation with Washington. Mr. Trump has vowed to “dismantle” the cartels and repeatedly raised the prospect of sending U.S. military forces into Mexico.

Under pressure from Mr. Trump, Ms. Sheinbaum’s government has intensified its nationwide crackdown on criminal groups. The Mexican authorities have arrested tens of thousands of people, seized hundreds of tons of drugs and destroyed thousands of clandestine labs and other sites used to make drugs. Mexico has also transferred dozens of drug trafficking suspects into U.S. custody.

Lynsey Chutel contributed reporting.
